title: Biomaterials and Tissue Engineering
description: Classes and properties of biomaterials, host responses and biocompatibility, sterilisation of implants, and principles of tissue engineering.

topics.title: Classes of Biomaterials
topics.summary: Metals, polymers, ceramics and composites and their medical uses.

notes.b: A biomaterial is a material designed to interact with biological systems for a medical purpose. Metals are strong and tough: 316L stainless steel (fracture plates, screws, temporary devices), cobalt–chromium alloys (joint replacements, wear-resistant), and titanium and its alloys (Ti-6Al-4V — dental implants, hip stems; excellent corrosion resistance and osseointegration, lower stiffness than steel). Nitinol (nickel–titanium) has shape memory and superelasticity (stents, orthodontic wires). Ceramics are hard, wear-resistant and brittle: alumina and zirconia (femoral heads), bioactive ceramics — hydroxyapatite and bioactive glass (bond to bone, coatings) — and resorbable tricalcium phosphate (bone graft substitutes).

Polymers are versatile: ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE — acetabular cup liners), polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA — bone cement, intraocular lenses), silicone (catheters, breast implants, shunts), polyurethane (catheters), PTFE/ePTFE (vascular grafts), polyester (Dacron grafts, sutures), hydrogels (contact lenses, wound dressings), and biodegradable polymers — polylactic acid (PLA), polyglycolic acid (PGA) and their copolymer PLGA — for absorbable sutures, screws and drug delivery. Composites combine materials (e.g. carbon-fibre-reinforced polymers, dental composites of resin with ceramic fillers).

topics.title: Mechanical and Surface Properties
topics.summary: Stress–strain behaviour, stiffness, fatigue, wear, corrosion and stress shielding.

notes.b: Stress = force ÷ area; strain = change in length ÷ original length. In the elastic region stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law); the slope is the Young's modulus (elastic modulus, stiffness). Beyond the yield point, plastic deformation occurs; ultimate tensile strength is the maximum stress; ductility is the extent of plastic deformation before fracture; toughness is energy absorbed before failure. Implants experience cyclic loading and can fail by fatigue below their static strength. Stress shielding occurs when a much stiffer implant (e.g. metal hip stem, modulus ~110–200 GPa versus cortical bone ~15–20 GPa) carries most of the load, so surrounding bone resorbs (Wolff's law), risking loosening.
k: Stress shielding: stiff implant → bone resorption
Wolff's law: bone adapts to load

notes.b: Surface chemistry, roughness, charge and wettability control protein adsorption and cell attachment — the first events after implantation. Metals may corrode (galvanic corrosion between dissimilar metals, crevice and pitting corrosion); titanium's passive oxide layer resists corrosion. Wear of articulating surfaces releases particles (e.g. polyethylene debris) that trigger macrophage-mediated osteolysis and aseptic loosening. Polymers may degrade by hydrolysis or oxidation; degradation products must be non-toxic. Surface modification (coatings, plasma treatment, hydroxyapatite spraying, drug-eluting layers) improves integration or reduces infection and thrombosis.

topics.title: Host Response and Biocompatibility
topics.summary: Inflammation and foreign-body reaction, blood compatibility, infection, and biocompatibility testing.

notes.b: Biocompatibility is the ability of a material to perform with an appropriate host response in a specific application. After implantation: injury and blood–material interaction (protein adsorption, provisional matrix), acute inflammation (neutrophils), chronic inflammation (macrophages, lymphocytes), granulation tissue, foreign-body reaction (macrophages fuse into foreign-body giant cells on the surface) and fibrous encapsulation. Blood-contacting devices (stents, heart valves, catheters) risk thrombosis via protein adsorption, platelet adhesion and coagulation activation — managed with anticoagulants/antiplatelets and surface treatments (heparin coating). Device-associated infection is promoted by biofilm formation (e.g. Staphylococcus epidermidis), which protects bacteria from antibiotics and immune cells, often requiring device removal.
k: Foreign-body giant cells and fibrous capsule
Biofilm infections often need device removal

notes.b: Biocompatibility is evaluated under the ISO 10993 series according to the nature and duration of body contact: tests include cytotoxicity (in vitro cell culture), sensitisation, irritation, systemic toxicity, genotoxicity, implantation, haemocompatibility (for blood contact) and carcinogenicity for long-term implants. Tests start in vitro, then animal studies, then clinical investigations. Regulatory approval (e.g. NAFDAC in Nigeria, FDA, CE marking) depends on risk class; post-market surveillance monitors failures (e.g. recalls of metal-on-metal hips).

topics.title: Sterilisation of Implants and Devices
topics.summary: Sterilisation methods and their effects on materials, packaging and reprocessing.

notes.b: Implants must be sterile (SAL 10⁻⁶). Steam autoclaving (121–134 °C) suits metals and heat-resistant items but can damage many polymers. Ethylene oxide gas sterilises heat-sensitive polymers and complex devices at low temperature, but requires aeration to remove toxic residues. Gamma irradiation and electron-beam sterilisation are widely used for single-use devices; they can cause polymer chain scission or cross-linking (e.g. gamma-irradiated UHMWPE in air oxidises — now irradiated in inert atmosphere and stabilised, sometimes with vitamin E). Hydrogen peroxide gas plasma is a low-temperature method for heat- and moisture-sensitive instruments. Dry heat suits glass and some metals. Material compatibility must be validated because sterilisation can alter mechanical properties, colour and degradation rate.
k: Gamma: single-use devices; may oxidise polymers

notes.b: Sterile barrier packaging maintains sterility until use; package integrity and expiry (event-related or time-related) are checked before use. Endotoxin (pyrogen) testing is required for implants and blood-contacting devices. Reprocessing single-use devices is discouraged because of infection, performance and legal risks. Reusable surgical instruments pass through a central sterile services department (CSSD): cleaning (the most important step — sterilisation cannot overcome inadequate cleaning), inspection, packaging, sterilisation, storage and traceability.
k: Cleaning is the critical first step in CSSD

topics.title: Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine
topics.summary: Cells, scaffolds and signals; stem cells; engineered tissues; 3-D printing and drug delivery.

notes.b: Tissue engineering combines cells, scaffolds and signals (growth factors, mechanical cues) to repair or replace tissues — the 'tissue engineering triad'. Scaffolds should be biocompatible, biodegradable at a rate matching tissue growth, porous and interconnected (pores of roughly 100–400 µm for bone ingrowth) and mechanically appropriate; materials include collagen, fibrin, alginate, chitosan, PLGA, polycaprolactone and bioceramics. Bioreactors provide nutrients and mechanical stimulation. Successful products include engineered skin substitutes for burns and chronic wounds, cartilage repair with autologous chondrocytes, and bone grafts.
k: Scaffold: biodegradable, porous (~100–400 µm for bone)

notes.b: Stem cells self-renew and differentiate. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent (ethical concerns); adult stem cells (e.g. mesenchymal stem cells from bone marrow or fat, haematopoietic stem cells) are multipotent; induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) are reprogrammed adult cells (Yamanaka factors). Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is an established therapy (e.g. curative for sickle cell disease in selected patients). Emerging tools include 3-D bioprinting, organoids, decellularised organ scaffolds and controlled drug-delivery systems (biodegradable microspheres, drug-eluting stents, transdermal patches). Regulation and ethics govern clinical use.
k: HSCT can cure sickle cell disease
